property_summary: For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether, the reference C accepts the call (does not revert) and updates pastBlockTime (observable via getter), whereas the mutant requiring 11 ether will revert for that same input—so calling fallback with 10 ether always succeeds on the reference but can fail on the mutant.

For any caller and any block timestamp strictly greater than the contract's stored pastBlockTime, calling the fallback with exactly 10 ether succeeds (does not revert) and thus the reference contract always accepts a 10 ether call while the mutant that requires 11 ether will revert for that input (so the property is broken by the mutant).

For any caller and block timestamp, the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime when the call sends exactly 10 ether and the current block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime; the mutant (which removes the timestamp check) will update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp is equal to pastBlockTime, so there exist inputs (calls at the same timestamp sending 10 ether) that make the mutant differ.

For any caller and any block timestamp, when a call to fallback sends exactly 10 ether the reference C only updates pastBlockTime if block.timestamp > pastBlockTime; the mutant (which removes that check) can update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp == pastBlockTime, so calling fallback twice within the same block with 10 ether will leave C.pastBlockTime unchanged after the second call (fails the mutant).

For any caller and any amount, whenever fallback is invoked sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract updates pastBlockTime only if block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime (so two calls sending 10 ether within the same block do not advance pastBlockTime twice); the mutant (which removes the timestamp check) will advance pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp equals the previous value, so repeated calls in the same block can change pastBlockTime in the mutant but not in the reference.

For any caller and any block timestamp, if a call to fallback sends exactly 10 ether and block.timestamp is not greater than C.pastBlockTime (i.e. equal), then the reference contract will NOT change pastBlockTime while the mutant (which removed the timestamp check) can change it; thus calling fallback twice in the same block with 10 ether should leave C.pastBlockTime unchanged after the second call on the reference but may change on the mutant.

For any caller and block, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether never changes C.pastBlockTime if block.timestamp is equal to its current value; the mutant (which removes the timestamp check) can update pastBlockTime when timestamp is equal, so there exist inputs (two calls within the same block sending 10 ether) that make the mutant differ.

After any successful call to fallback with exactly 10 ether and a caller that does not revert, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp, whereas the mutant can leave pastBlockTime unchanged when a transfer to the caller occurs (i.e., when block.number % 15 == 0 and the caller accepts the transfer).

For every successful call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp after the call; the mutant can violate this when it sends Ether to a cooperating (non-reverting) caller during the fallback, causing pastBlockTime to remain stale for some inputs.

For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, contract C always updates pastBlockTime to block.timestamp after the call; the mutant can violate this when the fallback transfers out (on block.number % 15 == 0) to a recipient that accepts the Ether, causing pastBlockTime to remain unchanged.

For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime where the callee REVERTS when sent Ether, C will still update pastBlockTime (because transfer to a reverting recipient does not succeed), but the mutant can fail to update pastBlockTime when it performs the transfer before updating state and the recipient reverts (causing observable difference in pastBlockTime after the call).

For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the correct contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp after the call; the mutant can leave pastBlockTime unchanged when it transfers out before updating state and the recipient reverts (or accepts) causing a different post-call pastBlockTime for some inputs.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether at strictly increasing timestamps, the reference contract only drains its balance when block.number % 15 == 0; thus after any single such call the reference's balance is equal to 0 iff block.number % 15 == 0, but the mutant uses 16 instead and will differ for some block numbers (e.g. numbers divisible by 15 but not 16).

Whenever fallback is called with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp strictly increases, then if block.number % 15 == 0 the contract's balance becomes zero (reference sends entire balance), whereas the mutant that sends only msg.value may leave a non-zero contract balance for some inputs.

For any caller and any block timestamp increase where msg.value == 10 ether, if block.number % 15 == 0 then after calling fallback the reference contract's balance is zero (it forwards entire balance), whereas the mutant that only transfers msg.value may leave a non-zero contract balance; the test fuzzes caller and initial contract balance to find inputs where the mutant differs.

For any caller and any prior contract balance, when fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether, block.timestamp strictly increases, and block.number is a multiple of 15, the reference contract will forward the entire contract balance to the caller so that address(c).balance becomes 0; the mutant that only transfers msg.value may leave a non-zero balance, violating this property for some initial balances.

For any caller and any prior nonzero contract balance, if fallback is invoked with msg.value == 10 ether, block.timestamp strictly increases, and block.number % 15 == 0, then the reference contract forwards its entire balance leaving address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that forwards only msg.value can leave a nonzero balance — so the property is that after such a call address(c).balance == 0 (which the mutant violates for some initial balances).

Whenever fallback is called with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp strictly increases, if block.number % 15 == 0 and the caller is a contract whose receive() intentionally REVERTs when sent only msg.value (but would accept the entire forwarded balance), the reference C will end the call successfully (because transfer of entire balance to a non-reverting recipient succeeds) while the mutant that sends only msg.value can cause a different observable outcome (here: the transfer to a reverting recipient will revert/behave differently) — so the property is: for any caller contract that reverts on receiving exactly msg.value, a call that succeeds on the reference will revert on the mutant for some inputs.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp is strictly greater than pastBlockTime, the reference contract updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (so the getter pastBlockTime equals the call's timestamp); the mutant that omits this update can leave pastBlockTime unchanged, violating that property for some inputs.
